content: The diagnosis, control, and elimination of rabies in animals are critical objectives, alongside efforts to assist countries in strengthening their veterinary services, laboratories, surveillance systems, and reporting mechanisms. At the 2016 OIE World Assembly of Delegates, member countries committed to fostering political will and ensuring long-term societal dedication to the elimination of rabies. They urged the OIE and other stakeholders to prioritize the eradication of dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 as a matter of public interest. The Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC) is a leading registered charity dedicated to reducing the global burden of rabies. GARC played a pivotal role in establishing the Partners for Rabies Prevention, an informal group comprising major international agencies such as WHO, FAO, OIE, rabies collaborating centers, reference laboratories, animal welfare NGOs, networks of rabies experts, and industry representatives. This group has initiated various studies and projects, including reassessments of the global burden of dog-mediated rabies, global surveys on rabies notifiability, and the development of the Blueprint for Rabies Prevention and Control, which includes a stepwise approach to rabies elimination. World Rabies Day, initiated in 2006, aims to raise awareness and mobilize resources for the prevention of human rabies and the control of animal rabies. Global and regional activities have led to significant improvements in rabies control policies by governments. Educational courses have been developed, such as the Rabies Educator Certificate for community educators, the Animal Handling and Vaccination Certificate for animal health technicians, and the Community Health Care Certificate for healthcare professionals. Mission Rabies, an international NGO, implements rabies elimination programs in endemic regions, with flagship projects in Goa (India), Ranchi (India), and southern Malawi. These campaigns include mass dog vaccination, rabies education, community awareness, and surveillance of dog-mediated rabies. A smartphone app utilizing geospatial technology has been developed to enhance epidemiological assessments and direct teams to remote areas. By 2016, over 213,000 dogs were vaccinated, 540,000 children were educated about rabies, and 64 rabid dogs were confirmed positive. In Goa, financial support from the government and the establishment of FAT testing facilities have significantly improved rabies case reporting and testing. Since 2014, reported human rabies deaths in Goa have decreased from 17 to just one in 2016. Pilot campaigns have also been conducted in Sri Lanka, Uganda, and Tanzania to support effective field protocols for broader application. World Animal Protection, another international NGO, focuses on ending animal cruelty and managing free-roaming dogs in communities worldwide. Their Red Collar campaign (2011–2016) aimed to end inhumane culling of dogs in response to rabies outbreaks in countries like Bangladesh, China, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Tanzania. In Africa, they collaborate with the Kenyan government to pilot a national rabies elimination strategy and with Sierra Leone to develop a national rabies elimination and dog population management strategy. They also work with GARC in several African countries through PARACON and are active in Brazil, China, and Costa Rica to develop a One Health dog population management approach. PARACON, established in 2015, strengthens the capacity of rabies experts in Africa by merging the Southern and Eastern African Rabies Group with the African Rabies Expert Bureau. Through workshops and tools like the Rabies Blueprint and the stepwise approach to rabies elimination, PARACON supports countries in progressing toward the elimination of dog-mediated rabies. The new PARACON Epidemiological Bulletin enhances the collection and visibility of surveillance data necessary for monitoring control progress. In Latin America, the REDIPRA meeting is held biennially to review rabies control strategies and coordinate regional responses. The 15th REDIPRA meeting in Brazil in 2015 emphasized surveillance of the last sites of dog-mediated rabies. A subgroup for Andean countries was created to coordinate efforts in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. In the Asia-Pacific region, a tripartite workshop operationalized the One Health concept in member countries. WHO, the Institut Pasteur, and the University of Lausanne organized the first international training course on rabies surveillance and control for Asian countries in 2015, establishing networks of local champions. Similar courses have been held in Senegal, Cambodia, and Cameroon, with future plans for a course in Tehran for Middle Eastern and Central Asian countries. In Europe, the WHO Rabies Bulletin Europe, established in 1977, collects data from over 40 countries to report confirmed rabies cases in humans and animals quarterly. The European Union Rabies Subgroup assesses and provides recommendations on co-financed oral rabies vaccination (ORV) campaigns. Since 2008, the European Union Reference Laboratory for Rabies in France has organized annual meetings to standardize diagnostic techniques. The Middle East and Eastern Europe Rabies Expert Bureau (MEEREB), established in 2010, is an inter-regional network working to improve rabies control and prevention. Members met in 2015 to review the rabies situation and discuss the One Health approach against rabies. Future research priorities include improving the delivery of rabies interventions, developing innovative vaccines, and refining vaccination strategies to achieve 70% coverage of dog populations. Operational research should focus on rigorous protocols, unbiased sampling, and appropriate comparison groups. Applied research should explore integrating dog rabies control into broader health programs and evaluating the impact of bite prevention education.
